cards.title: Core QA distinctions
cards.summary: Fast definitions for terminology interviewers often use to check whether basic QA concepts are separated correctly.

rows.detail: Improve the way quality is built through standards, reviews, process, feedback, and prevention.
Evaluate work products or the product to identify quality problems.
Provide information about quality and risk; testing can reveal defects but cannot prove their absence.
Investigate the cause of a failure or defect and change code, configuration, data, or another implementation element.
Ask whether the product or work product satisfies specified requirements: are we building it correctly?
Ask whether the product is fit for intended use and stakeholder needs: are we building the right product?

cards.title: Seven testing principles
cards.summary: The seven principles are frequent foundation-level interview material and explain why testing must be selective and context-driven.

rows.detail: Tests can reveal failures and defects; passing tests cannot prove that no defects remain.
Except for very small finite spaces, select tests using risk, techniques, priorities, and constraints.

rows.term: Early testing saves time and money
rows.detail: Review requirements, designs, and risks early so defects are found before expensive rework.
A relatively small number of components often contains a large share of observed defects.

moreRows.detail: Repeated unchanged tests become less effective; revise data, scenarios, and coverage as the product changes.
The appropriate strategy depends on product, users, risks, lifecycle, technology, and constraints.
A technically correct system can still fail if it does not solve the right user or business problem.

cards.title: Test process / test activities
cards.summary: Know the activity names and the output of each one; they overlap and iterate rather than forming a strict waterfall.

rows.detail: Define objectives, scope, approach, resources, schedule, risks, metrics, and completion criteria.
Compare actual status with the plan and adjust priorities, scope, resources, or schedule when needed.
Study the test basis and identify testable features, risks, and test conditions.
Derive test cases, coverage items, expected results, and data/environment needs from test conditions.
Prepare procedures/scripts, suites, data, environments, and execution order.
Run tests, compare actual and expected results, record evidence, and investigate anomalies.

moreRows.detail: Summarize achieved coverage, unresolved risks, defect status, lessons, and reusable or archived testware.

cards.title: Test levels
cards.summary: A test level answers where the test object sits in the system decomposition; do not mix levels with test types or regression labels.

rows.detail: Functions, classes, modules, or components, usually tested in isolation or near isolation.
Interfaces and interactions between components, modules, services, or subsystems inside the product.
Behavior and quality of the complete system against system-level requirements and risks.
Interfaces between the system under test and external services, platforms, partner systems, or protocols.
Evidence that the system is acceptable for users, business, contractual, operational, or regulatory needs.

cards.title: Test types
cards.summary: A test type answers what objective or quality question is being evaluated; the same type can be applied at several test levels.

rows.detail: Evaluate functions, business rules, calculations, permissions, flows, and other specified behavior.
Evaluate quality characteristics such as performance, reliability, security, compatibility, interaction capability, or safety.
Derive tests without using internal code structure; focus on inputs, outputs, rules, states, and observable behavior.
Derive tests from code or architecture structure, for example statements, branches, conditions, or paths.

moreRows.detail: Example: a security-focused system-integration test can be non-functional, automated, regression-focused, and black-box at the same time.

cards.title: Static vs dynamic testing
cards.summary: Static and dynamic describe whether the test object is executed, not a test level or a quality characteristic.

rows.meaning: No execution of the test object
rows.detail: Evaluate requirements, designs, code, test cases, or other work products through reviews or static analysis.
Run software or a system, observe behavior, and compare results with expectations or other oracles.
It can find ambiguity, inconsistency, unreachable code, standards violations, and design problems before runnable software exists.
It reveals runtime failures involving behavior, timing, integration, state, environment, data, and resource usage.

cards.title: Confirmation vs regression
cards.summary: After a change, confirmation proves the reported failure is fixed; regression looks for unintended side effects elsewhere.

rows.detail: Re-run the previously failing scenario and relevant variants against the fixed build.
Check previously working behavior that may be affected by the change.
Use changed code/configuration, dependencies, shared data, interfaces, and adjacent business flows to select regression scope.
Prioritize high-impact and high-likelihood consequences instead of automatically executing every historical test.

moreRows.detail: A defect can be correctly fixed while the change introduces a new defect somewhere else.

cards.title: Smoke vs sanity
cards.summary: These industry labels are not universally standardized, so explain the purpose you use rather than arguing about one absolute definition.

rows.detail: A small set of critical checks that decides whether a build or environment is stable enough for deeper testing.
A targeted check around a small change or area to decide whether more detailed testing is worthwhile.
Application starts, login works, core navigation loads, critical API/dependency is reachable, core transaction can complete.
State your team's convention and the decision each suite supports; acknowledge that organizations use the labels differently.

cards.title: Test design approaches & technique families
cards.summary: Start from the formal family name, then name the techniques; this is the interview-friendly map for choosing how tests are derived.

rows.detail: Derive tests from requirements, rules, models, interfaces, and observable behavior; includes EP, BVA, decision tables, and state transitions.
Derive tests from internal structure; common foundation examples are statement and branch coverage.
Use tester knowledge and learning; includes error guessing, exploratory testing, and checklist-based testing.
Derive shared examples with stakeholders, for example user-story collaboration, acceptance criteria, and ATDD.

moreRows.detail: Positive/negative, manual/automated, smoke/regression, and test levels describe other dimensions and should not be presented as peer design techniques.

cards.title: Equivalence Partitioning
cards.summary: Divide a large input or state domain into partitions expected to behave similarly, then choose representative values from each meaningful partition.

rows.detail: Identify valid and invalid classes based on actual rules or expected behavior.
If age must be 18–65: partitions are <18, 18–65, and >65; representative values might be 17, 30, and 66.
Partition coverage = exercised identified partitions ÷ total identified partitions × 100%.
Two values belong to the same partition only when there is a reason to expect equivalent behavior.

moreRows.detail: Partition fields separately, then use risk or combination techniques instead of testing the entire Cartesian product.

cards.title: Boundary Value Analysis
cards.summary: Focus on values around behavior-changing boundaries because implementation errors frequently occur at inclusive and exclusive limits.

rows.detail: Identify where behavior changes between partitions and exercise values on and around those boundaries.
For valid 18–65, exercise the closest values across each edge: 17, 18 and 65, 66.
Exercise below / on / above each boundary: 17, 18, 19 and 64, 65, 66.
Dates, string length, file size, retries, quotas, pagination, timeouts, and list sizes also have boundaries.

moreRows.detail: EP identifies the partitions; BVA intensifies testing at the borders between them.

cards.title: Decision Table Testing
cards.summary: Use a decision table when outcomes depend on combinations of conditions; it makes hidden or contradictory business-rule combinations visible.

rows.detail: List conditions, feasible combinations of their values, and the expected actions for each rule column.
Independent business inputs or predicates such as authenticated?, premium?, limit exceeded?.
Observable outcomes such as allow, deny, discount, require verification, or create a record.
Decision-table coverage = executed feasible rules ÷ identified feasible rules × 100%.

moreRows.detail: Collapse combinations only when a condition truly cannot affect the outcome for that rule.
Requirements full of if / and / or / unless logic are strong candidates for a decision table.

cards.title: State Transition Testing
cards.summary: Use state-transition testing when the same event can behave differently depending on current state or previous events.

rows.detail: Model states, triggering events, resulting states, and observable actions.
Exercise required transitions, for example Draft → Submitted after Submit.
Try events that must be rejected or ignored from a given state, for example Approve while still Draft.
Cover history-dependent flows such as retry, reopen, timeout, cancel, duplicate event, lockout, and recovery.

moreRows.detail: A common measure is executed valid transitions ÷ identified valid transitions × 100%, supplemented by risky sequences.

cards.title: Experience-based techniques
cards.summary: Use tester experience deliberately: the technique should guide where to look, while the mission and evidence remain visible.

rows.detail: Target likely defects using defect history, architecture knowledge, edge cases, and common implementation mistakes.
Learning, test design, and execution happen together while the tester adapts based on observations.
Use reusable quality or risk prompts while leaving the tester freedom to choose concrete checks.
A concise mission such as: Explore checkout recovery after network interruption, focusing on duplicate orders and stale totals.

moreRows.detail: Structured black-box techniques plus experience-based discovery usually provide stronger evidence than either alone.

cards.title: Good requirement characteristics
cards.summary: A strong interview answer checks both the wording of one requirement and whether the set of requirements works coherently together.

rows.detail: A reasonable reader should not be able to derive several different intended behaviors.
There must be observable evidence that can decide whether the requirement is satisfied.
Required conditions, inputs, outcomes, errors, boundaries, and constraints are present where needed.
The requirement is achievable within real constraints and exists for a stakeholder, business, regulatory, or system need.
It expresses one main obligation rather than several unrelated behaviors joined together.
It does not contradict known rules and its origin plus downstream consequences can be recovered.

moreRows.detail: Also check the set for completeness, consistency, non-duplication, coherent terminology, correct decomposition, modifiability, and quality constraints.
Fast, intuitive, appropriate, normally, should, supports, and etc. need measurable or contextual meaning.

cards.title: Test case structure
cards.summary: Interview answers should focus on reproducibility and purpose rather than treating every test case as a mandatory long template.

rows.detail: What rule, risk, behavior, or condition the test is checking.
Required account, permissions, configuration, system state, build, or dependency state.
Exact values or a clear generation rule; include meaningful valid, invalid, and boundary data.
The minimal reproducible manual sequence or automated/API operation needed to trigger the behavior.
A concrete observable outcome in UI, API response, state, event, log, database, or absence of change.

moreRows.detail: Cleanup, environment, priority, links, and evidence are useful when they improve repeatability or diagnosis.
Vague expectations such as works correctly and long click-by-click scripts that add no testing intent.

cards.title: Test documentation / testware
cards.summary: Test documentation is broader than test cases; know the artifacts and the decision or reproducibility need each one serves.

rows.detail: Defines objectives, scope, approach, resources, risks, criteria, responsibilities, estimates, and schedule for a test effort.
Record what needs evidence and the concrete inputs, preconditions, actions, and expected results used to obtain it.
Lighter-weight testware for recurring prompts or investigation where detailed scripts would be wasteful.
Group tests for a purpose and preserve the state/configuration required to reproduce execution.
Record actual outcomes, evidence, failures, anomalies, and information needed for investigation.
Communicate status against the plan, achieved evidence, deviations, unresolved defects, and residual risk.

moreRows.detail: Links test basis → conditions/cases → results/defects so coverage and change impact can be reasoned about.

cards.title: Test strategy vs plan vs approach
cards.summary: These terms are frequently collapsed in interviews; separate the scope and decision each one documents instead of memorizing one rigid template.

rows.detail: Defines high-level expectations, governance, or principles for testing across an organization or product family.
Defines a broader approach for obtaining quality evidence across a product, programme, or long-lived initiative.
Defines how and when objectives will be achieved for a project, release, iteration, migration, or major change.
Selected levels, types, techniques, priorities, exploratory work, automation, independence, data, and environments.
Places activities, dependencies, milestones, and execution order in time.

moreRows.detail: Context, test basis, scope, objectives, risks, responsibilities, approach, environment/data/tools, entry/exit criteria, metrics/reporting, estimates, resources, schedule, and dependencies.

cards.title: Defect lifecycle
cards.summary: Know the normal state flow but emphasize that exact statuses depend on the workflow; what matters is ownership and a verifiable resolution path.

rows.detail: A problem is reported with enough evidence for triage and investigation.
Impact, validity, ownership, priority, and next action are agreed.
The cause is addressed and a candidate fix becomes available for verification.
QA or another responsible party confirms the original failure no longer occurs in the intended build/environment.
The resolution is accepted and the workflow is complete.

moreRows.detail: Rejected / not a bug, duplicate, cannot reproduce, deferred, won't fix, reopened, blocked, or needs more information.
Use when the original issue still exists, the fix is incomplete, or the agreed acceptance condition is not satisfied.

cards.title: Severity vs priority
cards.summary: Severity describes impact; priority describes when the organization chooses to address the issue.

rows.detail: Evaluate user, business, data, security, safety, and operational impact plus the availability of a workaround.

rows.meaning: How soon should it be addressed?
rows.detail: Affected by release timing, exposure, strategic value, customer commitments, dependencies, and cost.
A severe failure in a disabled, obsolete, or inaccessible path may legitimately be deferred.
A minor but highly visible issue can be urgent for a launch, legal text, or important customer demo.

moreRows.detail: Use the project's documented severity and priority definitions; labels such as blocker/critical/major are not universal.

cards.title: Good defect report
cards.summary: Optimize a defect report for reproduction, diagnosis, and impact assessment rather than form completion.

rows.detail: State object + observed failure + useful condition, for example: Checkout remains on Payment after successful authorization.
Exact version, environment, browser/device, role, configuration, feature flags, and relevant timestamp.
Capture the state and inputs required to reproduce the problem.
Provide the shortest reliable sequence that triggers the failure; remove irrelevant navigation.
Describe the observable discrepancy and the basis for the expected behavior.
Attach useful logs, request/response, screenshot/video, IDs, DB/event evidence, reproducibility, affected users, and workaround.

moreRows.detail: Put observed behavior in the title unless the technical cause has actually been demonstrated.

cards.title: Traceability / RTM & change impact
cards.summary: Traceability is useful when it answers coverage, origin, or change-impact questions; a giant spreadsheet is not the goal.

rows.detail: Requirement / risk → derived requirements or acceptance criteria → test conditions → tests → results and defects.
Test, implementation, or lower-level requirement → the requirement, risk, or stakeholder need that justifies it.
Identify important requirements or risks that have evidence and those that remain uncovered.
When a requirement or implementation changes, find dependent requirements, tests, automation, data, interfaces, and risks.

moreRows.detail: A requirements traceability matrix is one implementation; IDs, links, issue relationships, or automated metadata can provide the same capability.
Incorrect traceability creates false confidence, so keep links minimal, meaningful, and maintainable.

cards.title: Quality characteristics
cards.summary: Use canonical quality-characteristic names in interviews, then translate each one into practical testing questions.

rows.detail: Functional completeness, correctness, and appropriateness for intended tasks.
Time behavior, throughput, capacity, and resource utilization under relevant load.
Coexistence and interoperability with required systems, platforms, and environments.
Recognizability, learnability, operability, error protection, engagement, inclusivity, and accessibility of interaction.
Availability, fault tolerance, recoverability, and behavior over time or under faults.

moreRows.detail: Confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, authenticity, and resistance to misuse.
Modularity, reusability, analyzability, modifiability, and testability of change.
Adaptability, scalability, installability, and replaceability across environments or changing needs.
Risk of harm, safe behavior, hazard identification, fail-safe behavior, and operational constraints where relevant.

cards.title: Acceptance, UAT, alpha & beta
cards.summary: These labels overlap in real projects, so distinguish the test level, the stakeholder purpose, and who performs the testing.

rows.detail: A test level that evaluates whether the system is acceptable against user, business, contractual, operational, or regulatory criteria.
Acceptance testing from the customer or user perspective to confirm real business work can be completed.
Controlled pre-release testing performed at or for the developing organization, often by internal or invited users.
Pre-release use by selected external users in realistic environments to expose issues and gather feedback.

moreRows.detail: Alpha and beta can contribute acceptance evidence, but neither automatically replaces explicit acceptance criteria or release authorization.

cards.title: Static reviews & static analysis
cards.summary: Know the major review forms and separate human review techniques from tool-based static analysis.

rows.detail: A lightweight review with little prescribed process; useful for quick feedback on low-risk work.
Usually author-led; the author explains the work product while participants ask questions and provide feedback.
Qualified peers assess technical suitability, alternatives, consistency, risks, or standards compliance.
A formal review with defined roles, preparation, entry criteria, defect logging, moderation, and follow-up.
Tools examine code or models for properties such as control/data flow, complexity, unreachable code, dependency rules, or security findings.

cards.title: Statement vs branch coverage
cards.summary: Coverage tells you which implementation structure was exercised; it does not prove that assertions, requirements, or test data are good.

rows.detail: Executed executable statements ÷ total executable statements × 100%.
Executed branches / decision outcomes ÷ total branches × 100%.
100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage for the measured code; the reverse is not guaranteed.
An if body may execute and give full statement coverage while the false branch is never tested.

moreRows.detail: High code coverage can coexist with weak assertions, missing requirements, wrong data, and untested integration behavior.

cards.title: Requirements-to-requirements relationships
cards.summary: Requirements are a graph, not a flat list; interview-ready review includes decomposition, dependencies, conflicts, and overlap between requirements.

rows.detail: A lower-level requirement makes a higher-level need more concrete while preserving its intent.
A broad capability is decomposed into smaller requirements that together implement the parent.
One requirement only makes sense or can operate when another requirement or condition is satisfied.
One requirement limits another or two requirements affect the same state, data, interface, or workflow.
Requirements may be mutually incompatible or duplicate the same rule with inconsistent wording.

moreRows.detail: When one requirement changes, review its parents, children, dependencies, interacting rules, acceptance criteria, and linked tests.

cards.title: Entry, exit, suspension & resumption criteria
cards.summary: Criteria should trigger real decisions about whether testing can start, continue, stop, or be considered sufficiently complete.

rows.detail: Conditions required to begin useful testing: valid build, environment/data ready, test basis usable, dependencies available, blockers understood.
Evidence needed to consider objectives sufficiently met: risk/coverage goals, defect state, key results, residual risk, required approvals.
Conditions that make continued testing wasteful or unsafe, such as an invalid build, broken environment, or unavailable critical dependency.
Specific evidence that the blocking condition has been resolved and test results can be trusted again.

moreRows.detail: A fully green but incomplete or low-value suite can still miss critical risk.

cards.title: Risk-based testing
cards.summary: Allocate earlier and deeper testing effort where product risk is highest, then make residual risk explicit when constraints force trade-offs.

rows.detail: A simple model is likelihood × impact; use the team's scale and avoid fake mathematical precision.
Complexity, novelty, many dependencies, code churn, weak observability, defect history, and unfamiliar technology.
Revenue, safety, security, data loss, legal exposure, user volume, blocked core tasks, and recovery cost.
Test earlier, with stronger techniques, broader data, more independence, and more focused regression.

moreRows.detail: Product risk threatens product quality/outcomes; project risk threatens delivery or testing through time, people, environments, tooling, or dependencies.

cards.title: Test prioritization under time pressure
cards.summary: When everything cannot be tested, make the selection logic and resulting residual risk explicit instead of pretending coverage is unchanged.

rows.detail: Deployment/startup, authentication, data access, payments/core workflow, and critical integrations.
The direct change plus dependencies and known regression hotspots.
Highest-value, highest-volume, or highest-consequence end-to-end paths.
Confirm high-impact fixes and run targeted regression around the affected area.
Expand by remaining risk, usage, defect history, and available time.

moreRows.detail: Record what was not tested and the risk that is being accepted.

cards.title: Test pyramid & testing quadrants
cards.summary: These are planning heuristics, not laws; use them to explain feedback speed, scope, and the different purposes of technical and business-facing testing.

rows.detail: Prefer many fast lower-level checks, fewer service/integration checks, and a smaller number of expensive UI end-to-end checks when the architecture supports it.
Optimize feedback speed, diagnosability, maintenance cost, and coverage—not a fixed percentage at each layer.
A collaboration model that distinguishes technology-facing vs business-facing and support-the-team vs critique-the-product activities.
Neither model replaces risk analysis; a product can legitimately need more integration, hardware, visual, accessibility, or end-to-end evidence.

cards.title: Test oracle: how do you know it is correct?
cards.summary: When an expected result is unclear, identify a credible source of truth before adding more test execution.

rows.detail: An explicit business rule or specified expected behavior.
A trusted existing implementation, simulator, validated previous version, or external authoritative system.
Recompute using a separate formula or model instead of copying the implementation logic under test.
A property that must always hold or an authoritative law, protocol, accounting, safety, or business constraint.

moreRows.detail: Useful for UX, visual quality, exploratory work, or other areas where exact automatic oracles are difficult; define reviewer expectations where possible.
A test can execute successfully while proving little if nobody can explain why the observed result should be considered correct.

cards.title: Agile, shift-left & CI
cards.summary: The core idea is faster, cheaper feedback and shared quality ownership—not merely moving the same manual tests earlier.

rows.detail: Challenge ambiguity, examples, acceptance criteria, risks, testability, observability, and dependencies before coding.
Review design/code, pair on tests, validate contracts, and add component/API checks close to the change.
Run fast deterministic checks on each relevant change; failures should be owned, diagnosable, and acted on quickly.
Use monitoring, synthetic checks, canaries, feature flags, and rollback signals as additional evidence after deployment.

moreRows.detail: Developers, testers, product, operations, security, and domain experts contribute different types of quality evidence.

cards.title: Release readiness / go-no-go evidence
cards.summary: A release decision is a risk decision supported by evidence; pass percentage alone is not a sufficient release argument.

rows.detail: Required user and business journeys pass in the relevant release candidate and environment.
Changed areas and dependencies received appropriate confirmation and regression evidence.
Known defects are understood by impact, exposure, workaround, and release consequence.
Untested or partially tested areas, assumptions, environment gaps, and known limitations are visible to decision-makers.
Monitoring, rollback/feature flags, migration/recovery, support, and runbook needs are ready where relevant.

cards.title: QA metrics that answer a decision
cards.summary: Start with the decision or question, then choose a metric; raw counts without denominator, scope, or context are easy to misuse.

rows.detail: Executed vs planned relevant scope, preferably split by feature, risk, environment, or release objective.
Open/closed trend, impact, age, reopen rate, or escaped defects where those measures support a decision.
Requirements, risks, techniques, code, platforms, or other coverage—always state what the denominator means.
Flaky tests, environment failures, automation reliability, build/deploy health, and recurring blocker causes.

moreRows.detail: Number of test cases, bugs found, or automation percentage alone is not a product-quality score.
Pair metrics with timeframe, denominator, scope, trend, and threshold or decision when applicable.

cards.title: Environment & test data triage
cards.summary: Before declaring a product defect, verify that build, configuration, dependency, or data drift is not explaining the observation.

rows.detail: Exact version, commit, artifact, container image, and deployment timestamp.
Feature flags, URLs, locale/timezone, caches, permissions, secrets wiring, and runtime settings.
Service versions, stubs/mocks, queues, third parties, database/schema migrations, and network reachability.
Account role, ownership, seed, prior mutations, clock-dependent state, cleanup, and concurrency conditions.
Align logs, traces, metrics, request IDs, events, and DB state around the same timestamp or correlation ID.

moreRows.detail: Prefer synthetic or masked data and least privilege when real personal or sensitive data is unnecessary.

cards.title: Root cause & defect prevention
cards.summary: A useful RCA goes beyond developer made a mistake and identifies what allowed the defect to be introduced and escape.

rows.detail: The failure that users, monitoring, or tests observed.
The immediate code, configuration, data, design, dependency, or infrastructure mechanism that produced the failure.
Why reviews, tests, monitoring, or release controls did not detect the problem earlier.
A weakness in requirements, process, architecture, ownership, tooling, environment, incentives, or feedback loops.
Change the system with clearer rules, safer defaults, automated checks, testability, observability, review prompts, or guardrails.

moreRows.detail: Use as a prompt, not a ritual; verify each causal link with evidence and allow multiple contributing causes.
